newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia sugar output seen on rising path.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia sugar output seen on rising path.

text.p: Australian raw sugar production is forecast to rise to 5.52 million tonnes in 1997/98 and then to 6.39 million tonnes in 2001/02, papers to be presented at the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) Outlook conference show.
Production in Australia in 1996/97 is seen at 5.33 million tonnes, up from 4.98 million tonnes the year before. The 1996/97 forecast is steady with ABARE's December forecast.
But world sugar prices are forecast to fall by almost 14.0 percent to average 10.8 U.S. cents a pound in 1996/97, with stocks at historically high levels.
Stocks are expected to decline from 1998/99 onwards, when world sugar consumption is projected to exceed production.
Sugar prices are projected to rise in real terms from 1998/99 to reach 11.2 U.S. cents a lb in 2001/02.

Australia's projected 2001/02 production would form part of world production of 135 million tonnes in that year, up from 124 million tonnes in 1996/97, a year when world production fell from the record 126 million tonnes of the year before.

Higher Australian production in 1996/97 flowed mainly from a five percent increase in area harvested, from slightly higher cane yields in Queensland where about 95.0 percent of Australia's sugar is produced, and from a higher sugar content of cane, ABARE said.
The value of Australian sugar exports are forecast to dip to A$1.36 billion in 1997/98 from A$1.42 billion the year before.
But ABARE expects Australian exports to rise in value to A$1.51 billion in 1998/99 and on to A$2.03 billion in year 2001/02.
Returns to Australian sugar producers are forecast to fall by nine percent in 1996/98 and average A$343.00 a tonne, largely because of lower world sugar prices.

On the medium-term outlook, ABARE said sugar production was expected to expand in key exporting countries such as Cuba, Brazil, Thailand and Australia, as well as in developing countries aiming for self-sufficiency.
